Mutation tools

4-mutation-tools.Rmd

Goal

Phase 4 turns the Phase 3 staging primitive into a usable surface for the LLM: nine mutation tools (add_block, remove_block, modify_block, add_link, remove_link, modify_link, add_stack, remove_stack, modify_stack) that the assistant can call to build and edit a board. Every tool is a thin façade over the Phase 3 stage API — its body constructs the relevant object (or forwards a delta), calls a stage_* function, and returns a short result string. No new dispatch path, no parallel reactive structure visible to the model: every mutation accumulates into the pending_update reactiveVal and flushes via the existing flush_pending hook on last_turn.

The phase deliberately pushes routing complexity down into blockr.core. A modify_block call ships a single partial-args delta as part of an update(...) payload; core decides whether to service it as an external-control write or as an atomic re-setup of the block server (see blockr.core#175). The consumer sees one shape and does not branch.

Scope

In:

  • Nine mutation tools, registered alongside the Phase 2 read tools via a new register_mutation_tools() helper.
  • A refactor of Phase 3’s stage_block_mod(), stage_stack_mod() and stage_link_mod() to accept a partial-args delta rather than a full constructed object — matching the unified dispatch shape agreed in blockr.core#175.
  • inst/examples/empty-board/ for manual smoke-testing against a live LLM.
  • Tests covering each tool’s happy path, the new delta-mod conflict rows, ID-generation behaviour, and a turn-boundary end-to-end test via shiny::testServer().

Out (deferred to later phases or out of roadmap):

  • Same-turn read-after-write. The Phase 2 read tools continue to read the committed board only. Staged operations are visible to the model only through its own tool-call history. Revisited if Phase 5 telemetry shows the model is confused.
  • A “pending changes” UI affordance (badge, diff preview, apply-now button). The reactiveVals are observable; an extension is cheap to bolt on later.
  • Snapshot / undo. Atomicity at the turn boundary is what we ship; multi-turn rollback waits on blockr.session hooks that do not yet exist.
  • Per-block-type custom tools. Block packages contributing tools (set_filter_expression, etc.) is a separate roadmap item.
  • Multi-board / multi-session orchestration. Extension state is scoped to the board it is mounted on.

Phase 4 is gated on the blockr.core change tracked at blockr.core#175: unified delta-shape mod slots for all three entity types (blocks, stacks, links), with blocks additionally routed internally to external-control writes vs. atomic re-setup. Until that lands, Phase 4 pins blockr.core via Remotes: to the branch carrying the fix. The design proceeds as if the unified dispatch is already available.

Architectural decisions

Trust core to dispatch; do not split routing in the consumer

The natural shape for modify_block(id, args) is one tool that ships one update(...) payload — and trusts the framework to do the right thing. Today (pre-#175) the framework forces consumers to choose: write external-control reactiveVals directly (bypassing update() entirely, fast but per-call cascade), or stage a blocks$mod entry that won’t actually re-run the server. Splitting that choice in every consumer of the mutation API leaks an implementation detail of blockr.core into every LLM-driven (or script-driven) board mutator.

Phase 4 takes the opposite stance. modify_block stages exactly one thing — a partial-args delta in pending_update$blocks$mod[[id]] — and flush_pending ships it via update(...). The core routing table (ctrl write if all changed args are ctrl-able on the live block; atomic re-setup otherwise) is core’s problem.

Two consequences shape the rest of this document:

  1. No pending_ctrl reactiveVal. Phase 3 left the door open for a parallel staging structure for ctrl writes (“if this turns out painful”). Phase 4 walks through that door and back out: the only staging structure for the whole tool surface is the update(...)-shaped pending_update from Phase 3. No sibling reactiveVals.
  2. The model sees uniform semantics. Every mutation tool returns "Staged <tool>(<id>) — will apply at turn end.". No tool fires side-effects mid-turn. The whole assistant turn is one atomic board update.

Mods are deltas; adds are full constructions

Mutation tools split into two shapes:

  • add_block, add_link, add_stack carry the full set of constructor arguments and produce a typed object (blockr.core::create_block(type, ...), new_link(...), new_stack(...)). The constructor call is the natural place to surface “missing required arg” / “wrong type” errors to the model, routed through with_tool_errors into a <tool> failed: <reason> string. Construction-as-validation: we have to construct the object to stage it anyway, so the validation is free.
  • modify_block, modify_stack, modify_link carry a partial-args delta (a named list of just the keys being changed). No construction in the consumer. The delta lands in pending_update$<entity>$mod[[id]] and flushes as part of the update(...) payload. Core merges the delta against the live entry, validates, and dispatches.

Why the asymmetry? An add knows everything (it’s bringing a new object into existence); a mod knows only the diff. For blocks and stacks, the current args live inside an opaque object — blockr.core does not export a block_args() readback, and stack subclasses (e.g. blockr.dock::dock_stack with its color attribute) make generic readback brittle. Forcing the consumer to reconstruct a full object for a one-arg change would require either a generic arg-readback API or a stateful mirror of every entity’s args inside the extension. Neither is worth the cost when core can do the merge in one place. Links are not subclassable today and could support full-replace from the consumer side, but Phase 4 puts them on the delta path too for API symmetry — every modify_* tool has the same body shape, every mod slot has the same payload shape.

This means stage-time validation for mods is shallow — at the consumer we can only check that the delta is a named list. The substantive validation (does n_rows exist on a head_block? is the proposed value the right type?) runs at flush against the live entry, in core. The cost: a typo’d arg name in modify_block goes undetected until turn end. The benefit: we don’t ship a parallel schema layer in the consumer that’s guaranteed to drift from blockr.core’s actual constructor signatures.

Block ids are immutable for committed blocks

The assistant cannot change the id of a block that already exists on the board. There is no change_id tool, no embedded id-change arg on modify_block, no path of any kind. Same for links and stacks.

The reasoning:

  • Ids are system identifiers, not user-facing labels. Blocks carry an id (the registry key) and a per-type display name registered via register_block(ctor, name, ...). The display name is type-level metadata, not per-instance editable surface; a “rename this block” user request maps onto changing the rendered label in the board UI (out of scope for Phase 4) or picking a different block type, not on changing the registry key. The conflation of “name” and “id” in casual speech is what makes this worth spelling out.
  • Stable ids = stable model context. The model is rebuilding its mental model of the board across turns from list_blocks / describe_block output. If ids could drift mid-conversation, the model’s tool-call history and current board state would desynchronise.
  • External references stay valid. Saved app state, bookmarks, upstream observers that key off block id, and any future blockr.session integration all assume committed ids are stable. The assistant’s mutation surface should not be the thing that breaks that.

For a staged (not yet committed) block, the id is freely changeable — but not via a dedicated tool. The model just stages a remove_block(old_id) followed by add_block(<type>, <args>, id = new_id). Behaviorally identical to re-keying the pending entry, costs two tool calls instead of one, and avoids a tool that has to detect “is this id pending vs. committed?” and dispatch differently.

If a user asks the assistant to change a committed block’s id, the expected handling is conversational: the assistant explains it can offer remove_block(old_id) + add_block(<type>, <args>, id = new_id), but that tears down the block server (lost eval state, re-evaluation of downstream blocks), and asks the user whether that’s acceptable. Phase 5’s prompt-context layer will likely codify this kind of guidance into the system prompt.

Same rule applies to link and stack ids. The conflict table has no id-change rows for any entity type.

Hybrid ID generation via blockr.core::rand_names()

add_block, add_link, add_stack all accept an optional id argument:

  • If the model supplies an id, it is used as-is. Uniqueness against the merged board-plus-pending state is checked by core’s validator at stage time (Phase 3’s validate_pending already runs the full validator chain). Format constraints are whatever core enforces — we do not layer our own.
  • If the model omits the id, the package generates one via blockr.core::rand_names(old_names = existing_ids(board, pending)). Core’s default rand_names produces adjective-animal ids (quick-elephant, tidy-otter) via the optional ids package, falling back to random letter strings. The tool result string echoes the final id in either path.

Result string template:

"Staged add_block(quick-elephant) — will apply at turn end."

The id is always present and unambiguous, so the model can quote it in subsequent calls without needing a separate listing tool.

Read tools stay committed-only (reaffirmed)

Phase 3’s deferred decision is settled in favour of option (1): read tools read board$board, not a merged board-plus-pending view. The reasons accumulated since Phase 3 still hold:

  • The stage-time validator already accounts for pending state when checking cross-references (e.g. an add_link(foo→bar) staged after an add_block(foo) validates against the merged payload thanks to validate_pending calling through to combine_update_blocks in core).
  • get_block_result cannot return a value for a pending block (no server has been built yet), so a partial merge view would create the illusion of a usable block.
  • The model’s own tool-call history records what it staged this turn — a separate “list pending” surface adds nothing the conversation log does not already carry.

If Phase 5’s user-test telemetry surfaces friction here, the lightweight fix is a new list_pending_changes() tool that explicitly reports the staged operations (not a retrofit of the existing read tools).

Validity checks delegated to core

Phase 3’s validate_pending(payload, board) runs the full validate_board_update chain on every stage. Cycles, dangling block references in links, missing target inputs, duplicate ids and the rest are caught there against the merged state. Phase 4 adds nothing new. The stagers stay thin: collapse against the conflict table, call commit_pending, return. There is no consumer-side re-implementation of any cross-reference rule.

Reject add → mod; recover via remove + add

Phase 3’s conflict table lenient-collapses add(x) followed by mod(x): the pending add’s value is replaced by the mod’s new value. In Phase 3 the mod carried a full block object, so the collapse was a trivial swap. In Phase 4 the mod carries a delta, and producing the collapsed value would require rebuilding the staged block with the merged args via create_block(type, merged_args). The original (type, args) recipe is known at stage time of the add_block call, but discarded once the block is stored — there is no public arg readback on a constructed block.

We could maintain a sidecar recipe cache (a second reactiveVal keyed by id holding list(type = ..., args = ...) for every staged add). It would close the gap and keep the row a collapse. The cost is a second reactiveVal that has to stay in lockstep with pending_update across every add and rm, plus a more complex stage_block_mod that branches on “is this a live-board target or a pending-add target?”.

Phase 4 takes the simpler trade. The add → mod row rejects. The model recovers by issuing remove_block(x) + add_block(type, corrected_args, id = "x") instead. The corrected args are visible to the model in its own tool-call history (the prior add_block call sits in the conversation log with the original type and args), so reconstructing them is not a knowledge problem.

The rejection error string points the model at the recovery path explicitly:

"modify_block(foo) failed: foo is staged for creation this turn.
 Use remove_block(foo) followed by add_block(<type>, <args>, id = \"foo\")
 with the corrected arguments."

Cost: extra tokens when the model self-corrects a pending-add mid-turn, especially for blocks with many args. The frequency is bounded (only triggers on same-turn second-thoughts about an add). Benefit: no second reactiveVal, no recipe bookkeeping, no divergence risk between the staged block and its recipe.

Same rule for stacks: add_stack(x) → modify_stack(x, ...) rejects. Base stacks expose stack_blocks() / stack_name() readers, but subclasses such as blockr.dock::dock_stack add extra attributes (e.g. color) without a generic readback API, so a recipe-free collapse is not portable across subclasses. Keeping the rule uniform across block and stack mods is also easier for the model to internalise than two different behaviours for two superficially-identical operations.

The one collapse that doesn’t need reconstruction is still in the table: add(x) → rm(x) drops the pending add. A trivial named-list manipulation, no recipe required.

Conflict table for delta-mods

Phase 3’s nine-row table for blocks extends with one row flip: add → mod becomes a reject (see previous section) rather than a collapse. The remaining collapses keep their Phase 3 mechanics except for mod → mod, where the collapse now merges deltas key-wise rather than replacing the full block.

For blocks ({add, mod, rm} × {add, mod, rm}):

Prior pending entry Stage call Outcome
add(x) add(x, ...) reject — duplicate id
add(x) mod(x, ...) reject — x is staged for creation; use remove_block + add_block with corrected args
add(x) rm(x) collapse — drop pending add
mod(x, d1) add(x, ...) reject — x exists on board, cannot re-add
mod(x, d1) mod(x, d2) collapse — pending mod becomes merge_args(d1, d2) (key-wise last-write-wins)
mod(x, d1) rm(x) collapse — discard pending mod, stage rm
rm(x) any (x, ...) reject — x is being removed

The merge_args(prev, new) helper is named-overwrite: keys in new replace prev; keys in prev not present in new survive. Matches “delta means partial override”.

Stacks and links follow the same table, substituting the appropriate modify_* tool name. All three entity types have an identical conflict shape now that links also surface a modify_* tool with delta semantics.

Principle inherited from Phase 3: collapse where the combined intent is unambiguous and cheap, reject otherwise (including the one Phase 4 reject — add → mod — that buys us no recipe cache).

Tool result formatting

All nine tools follow the same template:

"Staged <tool>(<id>) — will apply at turn end."

Same shape as Phase 3’s format_stage_error for failures ("<tool>(<id>) failed: <reason>") so the model parses one consistent pattern across the whole API.

No structured tool result (no JSON object). The model consumes the chat content of the tool result; a single sentence is enough for it to confirm the call landed and to recall the id later. Phase 5 may revisit this if richer telemetry helps the model self-correct.

Atomicity, errors, and flush rejection

Inherited from Phase 3 unchanged:

  • A turn’s mutations are atomic. Any stage error throws from the tool body, gets re-shaped by with_tool_errors, and goes back to the model as a <tool> failed: <reason> string. The pending payload is not mutated by a failing stage — the model can retry.
  • Flush rejection (validator throws at update(...) dispatch time) discards the whole staged payload and logs a warning. The user sees the standard Shiny notification from blockr.core’s validator; the model sees nothing on the next turn unless the user (or Phase 5’s prompt-context layer) tells it.
  • No partial apply on flush. Phase 4 changes nothing here.

Tool surface

Each tool factory has the Phase 2 shape: tool_<name>(board, update, pending, session) returns an ellmer::tool(...). Bodies below elide the with_tool_errors("<name>", { ... }) wrapper for brevity; assume each tool body is wrapped exactly like the Phase 2 read tools at R/tools-read.R.

add_block(type, args, id = NULL) 

tool_add_block <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(type, args, id = NULL) {

      id <- id %||% rand_names(existing_ids(board, pending, "blocks"))

      parsed <- jsonlite::fromJSON(args, simplifyVector = TRUE)
      block <- do.call(create_block, c(list(type), parsed))

      stage_block_add(pending, board, id, block)

      sprintf(
        "Staged add_block(%s) — will apply at turn end.", id
      )
    },
    name        = "add_block",
    description = paste(
      "Add a new block to the board. `type` is a block id as",
      "reported by list_available_blocks. `args` is a JSON object",
      "(passed as a string) of constructor arguments — field names",
      "must match the arg names reported by list_available_blocks",
      "for the chosen type. `id` is optional — if omitted,",
      "a unique id is generated."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      type = ellmer::type_string(
        "Block type id, from list_available_blocks."
      ),
      args = ellmer::type_string(
        paste(
          "JSON object of constructor arguments, e.g.",
          "'{\"n\": 10}'. Field names match list_available_blocks."
        )
      ),
      id = ellmer::type_string(
        "Optional id for the new block. Generated if omitted.",
        required = FALSE
      )
    )
  )
}

args ships as a JSON-formatted string rather than a native object because ellmer’s type_object requires a closed key list and the only escape hatch (.additional_properties = TRUE) is deprecated and only supported by Claude. A JSON-string parameter is provider-agnostic; the body parses with jsonlite::fromJSON and surfaces parse failures, construction failures (missing required arg, wrong type, unknown type id) through the <tool> failed: <reason> envelope. stage_block_add enforces uniqueness against board + pending via core’s validator and the conflict-table reject rows.

remove_block(id) 

tool_remove_block <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(id) {

      stage_block_rm(pending, board, id)

      sprintf(
        "Staged remove_block(%s) — will apply at turn end.", id
      )
    },
    name        = "remove_block",
    description = paste(
      "Remove a block from the board. Any links to or from the",
      "block are cleaned up at apply time by core; the model does",
      "not need to remove them explicitly."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      id = ellmer::type_string("Block id to remove.")
    )
  )
}

The cascade-cleanup of orphaned links and stack memberships is core’s job at preprocess_board_update time. The tool does not stage those; the model does not need to know they happen.

modify_block(id, args) 

tool_modify_block <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(id, args) {

      delta <- jsonlite::fromJSON(args, simplifyVector = TRUE)

      stage_block_mod(pending, board, id, delta)

      sprintf(
        "Staged modify_block(%s) — will apply at turn end.", id
      )
    },
    name        = "modify_block",
    description = paste(
      "Change one or more constructor arguments of an existing",
      "block. `args` is a JSON object (passed as a string) of",
      "just the keys being changed; unmentioned keys keep their",
      "current values."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      id = ellmer::type_string("Id of the block to modify."),
      args = ellmer::type_string(
        paste(
          "JSON object of arguments to change, e.g.",
          "'{\"n\": 5}'. Only supplied keys are modified."
        )
      )
    )
  )
}

Same JSON-string treatment as add_block for the same reason — ellmer cannot model an open-keyed object portably. stage_block_mod writes the parsed delta into pending$blocks$mod[[id]], collapses with a prior pending mod by key-wise merge, or rejects against a pending add / rm per the conflict table. No construction in the consumer.

add_link(from, to, input, id = NULL) 

tool_add_link <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(from, to, input, id = NULL) {

      id <- id %||% rand_names(existing_ids(board, pending, "links"))

      link <- new_link(from, to, input)

      stage_link_add(pending, board, id, link)

      sprintf(
        "Staged add_link(%s: %s → %s$%s) — will apply at turn end.",
        id, from, to, input
      )
    },
    name        = "add_link",
    description = paste(
      "Add a link that wires the output of block `from` into",
      "argument `input` of block `to`. Both blocks must exist on",
      "the board or be staged for creation in this turn."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      from  = ellmer::type_string("Source block id."),
      to    = ellmer::type_string("Destination block id."),
      input = ellmer::type_string(
        "Input slot on the destination block."
      ),
      id = ellmer::type_string(
        "Optional id for the new link. Generated if omitted.",
        required = FALSE
      )
    )
  )
}

Cross-reference validity (both blocks exist, input is a valid slot on to, no cycle introduced) is checked by core’s validator at stage time against the merged board-plus-pending state.

modify_link(id, from = NULL, to = NULL, input = NULL) 

tool_modify_link <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(id, from = NULL, to = NULL, input = NULL) {

      delta <- compact(list(from = from, to = to, input = input))

      stage_link_mod(pending, board, id, delta)

      sprintf(
        "Staged modify_link(%s) — will apply at turn end.", id
      )
    },
    name        = "modify_link",
    description = paste(
      "Retarget an existing link. Any combination of `from`, `to`,",
      "and `input` may be supplied; only supplied fields are",
      "changed. Omitted fields keep their current values."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      id = ellmer::type_string("Id of the link to modify."),
      from = ellmer::type_string(
        "New source block id.",
        required = FALSE
      ),
      to = ellmer::type_string(
        "New destination block id.",
        required = FALSE
      ),
      input = ellmer::type_string(
        "New input slot on the destination block.",
        required = FALSE
      )
    )
  )
}

add_stack(blocks, name = NULL, id = NULL) 

tool_add_stack <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(blocks, name = NULL, id = NULL) {

      id <- id %||% rand_names(existing_ids(board, pending, "stacks"))

      stack <- new_stack(blocks = blocks, name = name)

      stage_stack_add(pending, board, id, stack)

      sprintf(
        "Staged add_stack(%s) — will apply at turn end.", id
      )
    },
    name        = "add_stack",
    description = paste(
      "Group a set of blocks into a stack. `blocks` is a",
      "character vector of block ids; `name` is an optional",
      "human-readable label."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      blocks = ellmer::type_array(
        "Block ids to include in the stack.",
        items = ellmer::type_string()
      ),
      name = ellmer::type_string(
        "Optional display name for the stack.",
        required = FALSE
      ),
      id = ellmer::type_string(
        "Optional id for the new stack. Generated if omitted.",
        required = FALSE
      )
    )
  )
}

remove_stack(id)

modify_stack(id, blocks = NULL, name = NULL) 

tool_modify_stack <- function(board, update, pending, session) {

  ellmer::tool(
    function(id, blocks = NULL, name = NULL) {

      delta <- compact(list(blocks = blocks, name = name))

      stage_stack_mod(pending, board, id, delta)

      sprintf(
        "Staged modify_stack(%s) — will apply at turn end.", id
      )
    },
    name        = "modify_stack",
    description = paste(
      "Change a stack's member blocks and/or name. Either or both",
      "arguments may be omitted; only supplied fields are",
      "changed."
    ),
    arguments = list(
      id = ellmer::type_string("Stack id to modify."),
      blocks = ellmer::type_array(
        "New set of member block ids.",
        items    = ellmer::type_string(),
        required = FALSE
      ),
      name = ellmer::type_string(
        "New display name.",
        required = FALSE
      )
    )
  )
}

compact() is a small utility that strips NULL entries from a list — so a modify_stack call that supplies only name produces a delta list(name = ...) with no blocks key.

Stage API changes from Phase 3

The Phase 3 stagers take full constructed objects for mods. With the unified delta shape, the three mod stagers all change signature. No new stagers.

Function Phase 3 signature Phase 4 signature
stage_block_add (pending, board, id, block) unchanged
stage_block_mod (pending, board, id, block) (pending, board, id, delta)
stage_block_rm (pending, board, id) unchanged
stage_stack_add (pending, board, id, stack) unchanged
stage_stack_mod (pending, board, id, stack) (pending, board, id, delta)
stage_stack_rm (pending, board, id) unchanged
stage_link_add (pending, board, id, link) unchanged
stage_link_mod (pending, board, id, link) (pending, board, id, delta)
stage_link_rm (pending, board, id) unchanged

The internal conflict-handling in stage_block_mod becomes:

stage_block_mod <- function(pending, board, id, delta) {

  cur <- isolate(pending())

  if (id %in% names(cur$blocks$add)) {
    stage_abort(
      "modify_block", id,
      paste0(
        id, " is staged for creation this turn. Use remove_block(",
        id, ") followed by add_block(<type>, <args>, id = \"", id,
        "\") with the corrected arguments."
      )
    )
  }

  if (id %in% cur$blocks$rm) {
    stage_abort(
      "modify_block", id,
      "id is staged for removal; mod has no effect"
    )
  }

  new <- cur

  if (id %in% names(cur$blocks$mod)) {

    new$blocks$mod[[id]] <- merge_args(cur$blocks$mod[[id]], delta)

  } else {

    new$blocks$mod <- c(
      new$blocks$mod,
      set_names(list(delta), id)
    )
  }

  commit_pending(pending, isolate(board$board), new, "modify_block", id)
}

Two structural notes:

  • The type of pending$blocks$mod diverges from Phase 3’s typed blocks(...) object. Phase 4 stores it as a named list of deltas (each a named list of args), matching the post-#175 payload shape. The validator in commit_pending runs against this new shape — which requires the matching change in core (#175) to land before the test suite can pass end-to-end.
  • The merge_args helper is named-overwrite: merge_args(d1, d2) returns a list whose keys are the union, with values from d2 winning on conflict.

stage_stack_mod and stage_link_mod follow the same template with their entity-specific slot names and conflict-table guards. All three mod stagers have identical body shape; only the entity key differs (blocks, stacks, links).

Extension server diff 

asst_ext_srv <- function(system_prompt, messages) {

  function(id, board, update, ...) {

    moduleServer(
      id,
      function(input, output, session) {

        chat_ctor <- isolate(
          get_board_option_value("llm_model", session)
        )
        sys_prompt <- coal(system_prompt, default_system_prompt())

        client <- chat_ctor(system_prompt = sys_prompt)

        pending_update <- reactiveVal(empty_pending())

        register_read_tools(client, board, update, session)
        register_mutation_tools(                                    # new
          client, board, pending_update, session
        )

        if (length(messages)) {
          client$set_turns(
            lapply(messages, ellmer::contents_replay)
          )
        }

        mod <- shinychat::chat_mod_server("chat", client)

        observeEvent(
          mod$last_input(),
          {
            reset_pending(pending_update)
            record_new_turns()
          },
          ignoreNULL = TRUE
        )

        observeEvent(
          mod$last_turn(),
          {
            flush_pending(pending_update, update)
            record_new_turns()
          },
          ignoreNULL = TRUE
        )

        list(
          state = list(
            system_prompt = sys_prompt,
            messages      = messages
          )
        )
      }
    )
  }
}

No second reactiveVal beyond Phase 3’s pending_update. The extension carries exactly one piece of turn-local state for staging, mirroring Phase 3 unchanged.

Files added / changed

  • R/tools-mutation.R (new) — nine tool_* factories, the register_mutation_tools() helper, existing_ids(), merge_args(), compact().
  • R/staging.R — refactor stage_block_mod, stage_stack_mod and stage_link_mod to take a delta (instead of a full block / stack / link). Update empty_pending() so the three mod slots are plain list() (named lists of deltas) instead of Phase 3’s typed blocks() / links() / stacks() — the typed slots no longer fit the delta shape.
  • R/extension.R — call register_mutation_tools() from asst_ext_srv. No new reactiveVal.
  • tests/testthat/test-tools-mutation.R (new) — per-tool happy path; per-tool error path (construction failure on adds, conflict-table rejects); ID generation (model-supplied, omitted, collision).
  • tests/testthat/test-staging.R — extend with the new delta shape for stage_block_mod / stage_stack_mod / stage_link_mod; remove the Phase 3 tests that validate the full-object mod shape.
  • tests/testthat/test-extension.R — end-to-end turn-boundary test asserting one update(...) per turn carrying the expected shape for a multi-tool turn (add, link, mod).
  • inst/examples/empty-board/ (new) — minimal demo app exercising the full surface.
  • DESCRIPTION — bump Remotes: to pin blockr.core to the branch carrying the #175 fix; unpinning at release time. Add jsonlite to Imports: (used by add_block and modify_block tool bodies to parse the JSON-shaped args parameter; the other tools take typed top-level args and do not need it). jsonlite is already loaded transitively via ellmer, but the explicit declaration documents the direct use.

No new exports. The mutation tools are internal to the extension’s server scope, accessed only via register_mutation_tools.

Acceptance criteria

Automated (CI / devtools::check())

The end-to-end staging / flush assertions below are gated on the blockr.core change in issue 175. Until that lands, the tests pin blockr.core via Remotes: to the branch carrying the delta-shape mod dispatch; CI tracks that branch.

  • Per-tool happy path: each of the nine tools, called against a synthetic board fixture, stages the expected entry into pending_update and returns the expected result string.
  • Per-tool error path: at least one error case per tool, asserting the returned string starts with "<tool> failed: ". Coverage includes construction failure (missing required arg on add_*), conflict-table rejects (duplicate add, add → mod, anything on a staged-rm id), and unknown id for rm / mod.
  • ID generation: explicit valid id → used as-is; explicit colliding id → rejected via core’s validator; omitted id → rand_names generates a non-colliding id and the tool result echoes it.
  • Conflict-table coverage: one test per collapse row asserting the post-stage pending_update state; one test per reject row asserting the error string and that no state changed.
  • flush_pending test cases from Phase 3 continue to pass against the new payload shape (delta-mods).
  • shiny::testServer() end-to-end (scripted sequences invoke tool functions directly via client$get_tools(), simulating what ellmer’s dispatch loop would do on the model’s behalf):
    • A turn with add_block, add_link, add_stack flushes exactly one update(...) carrying all three.
    • A turn with add_block(foo, ...) then modify_block(foo, ...) returns a failure string for the modify, and the flushed update(...) carries only the original add (no mod entry for foo).
    • The recovery sequence flushes correctly: a turn scripted as add_block(foo, type, args1) → modify_block(foo, args2) (fails) → remove_block(foo) (collapses with pending add to a no-op) → add_block(foo, type, args3) flushes exactly one update(...) carrying a single add for foo with args3 and no rm.
    • Two last_turn firings without intervening stages produce zero update(...) calls.
  • Phase 1, 2, 3 acceptance criteria continue to pass.
  • devtools::check() passes 0/0/0.

Manual (demo app, live LLM)

A new example app at inst/examples/empty-board/: empty board, a single text input for the user prompt, no pre-loaded state. Used to smoke-test the full surface end-to-end against a real provider.

Scenarios to verify by hand:

  • Build a pipeline. “Load the iris dataset, drop the species column, then plot sepal length vs. width.” Expected: at turn end the board carries 3 blocks (e.g. dataset_block, subset_block, scatter_block), 2 links connecting them, and a 1-message chat transcript reporting each staged operation. No console errors.
  • Modify in place. Starting from the pipeline above: “change the dataset to mtcars.” Expected: modify_block routes through core’s ctrl path if the dataset arg is ctrl-able, or an atomic re-setup otherwise. Downstream blocks re-evaluate with the new data; the chat reports the staged modify only.
  • Id-change request from the user. “Rename dataset to data_source.” Expected: the assistant declines an id change on the committed block, explains it can offer remove_block + add_block (with the trade-off that the block’s eval state and outputs are torn down and re-evaluated), and asks the user whether to proceed.
  • Recover from a wrong arg. “Add a head block with 5 rows.” (model picks the wrong arg name). “Sorry, use n not rows.” Expected: the model’s first modify_block returns the is staged for creation this turn error; the model recovers by calling remove_block followed by add_block with the corrected args, and the flushed payload at turn end carries exactly one add with the corrected arg.

Manual checks are documentation, not gating — they verify the design holds in a real assistant loop and are recorded in the PR description.

Known limitations carried into later phases

  • Reads remain committed-only. No same-turn read-after-write. The model relies on its tool-call history for what it staged. Phase 5’s prompt-context layer or a future list_pending_changes() tool can add explicit visibility if empirical usage shows the need.
  • Stage-time mod validation is shape-only. Substantive validation of a delta (valid arg names, type compatibility) happens at flush via core’s validator chain, not at stage time. A typo’d arg name in modify_block flushes and rejects at turn end. The user sees the standard Shiny notification; the model hears about it only via the next turn’s user prompt (or via Phase 5’s prompt-context layer once it lands).
  • add → mod is a reject, not a collapse. Phase 3’s lenient in-turn self-correction does not extend to changing a staged add’s args. The model has to issue remove_block + add_block with corrected args. Cost is bounded (extra tokens in same-turn self-correction); benefit is no recipe cache or second reactiveVal in the extension. If empirical use shows the model has trouble with the recovery pattern, a future phase can reintroduce the collapse behind a sidecar recipe cache.
  • add_block / modify_block args are JSON-formatted strings, not native typed objects. ellmer’s type_object requires a closed key list, and the only escape hatch (.additional_properties = TRUE) is deprecated and supported only by Claude. JSON-string is the portable workaround. Trade-off: the model must format args as a JSON string rather than emitting a native object, and the tool body parses with jsonlite::fromJSON. The clean upgrade path — per-block-type tool generation backed by registry type info — is tracked in #12.
  • Stack subclass ctor args are unreachable from the assistant. add_stack(blocks, name, id) and modify_stack(id, blocks, name) expose only the base blockr.core::new_stack args, so e.g. the color attribute on blockr.dock::dock_stack cannot be set or modified through the assistant — it falls back to the auto-promoter’s default at apply time. Same architectural cause as #12 but applied to stacks; tracked separately in #13. Links face the same gap if subclasses are ever introduced (none today, so no urgency).
  • Pinned upstream Remotes:. Until the matching changes in blockr.core and blockr.dock are released, DESCRIPTION pins both via Remotes: to the PR branches: blockr.core#176 (delta-shape mod payload + update_link/update_stack generics) and blockr.dock#133 (stacked on #132, which fixes the two dock-side observer issues #131 and #130 surfaced during Phase 4 validation). Live end-to-end testing against Claude confirmed the pinned versions behave correctly: add_block / add_link / add_stack build pipelines, and modify_block against ctrl-able args updates the board in place without dock observer errors. Unpin at release time.
  • Stage-time link validator and apply-time preprocess disagree on dangling links (blockr.core). When the model removes a block whose existing links are still referenced elsewhere on the board, then tries to add a new link, the stage-time validate_board_update_xrefs rejects with "Expecting all links to refer to known block IDs." — even though preprocess_board_update would auto-clean the orphans at apply time. The model has to explicitly remove_link the dangling links before adding new ones. Tracked at blockr.core#177. Workaround on the assistant side could be to mirror preprocess’s orphan-cleanup in stage_block_rm; for now we prefer the upstream fix so behaviour stays single-source.
  • External-control writes still go through update(). This is the design’s bet on blockr.core#175. If core resolves the issue with a less-unified approach (e.g. ctrl writes still bypass update() and consumers must route), Phase 4 will need a carve-out in modify_block to route the ctrl-eligible subset directly. Tracked.
  • Atomic flush has no partial-success fallback. Inherited from Phase 3 unchanged: a racing user edit that invalidates the payload at dispatch time discards the whole turn’s mutations.
  • No snapshot / undo. Inherited from Phase 3 / roadmap.
